posts.title: Warren McCulloch, chairman [sic] of the Macy Conferences on Cybernetics, in a letter to the cybernetics group before the tenth and final conference, 1953. Discovered and shared by Sean Manion.
posts.description: Warren S. McCulloch's 1953 letter to the cybernetics group, ahead of the tenth and final Macy Conference, reviews the group's attempts to develop shared understanding across fields. It moves from feedback and purposive behaviour to communication, information, logic, and the limits of agreement. The public SysCoI post was substantively expanded on 15 November 2026: scans shared by Sean Manion now support a reading transcription of all 13 manuscript pages rather than the earlier three-page excerpt. The transcriber explains how handwritten changes, gaps, historical spelling, and ambiguous revisions have been handled. This is a reading transcription, not a diplomatic edition; historical scientific and medical statements are McCulloch's, not independently verified contemporary findings.

posts.title: Doing Serious Systems Thinking Means Getting Rid of Elephants, Icebergs and Leverage Points – Jackson (2026) on LinkedIn
posts.description: Michael C. Jackson criticises the blind-men-and-elephant, iceberg, and leverage-point metaphors when used to describe complex situations. He argues that they can imply an observer outside the situation, fixed boundaries or hierarchies of causes, and predictable interventions, overlooking plural perspectives, changing interactions, and recursive causation. His original LinkedIn argument appeared in October 2026. On 17 November, Integration and Implementation Insights (i2Insights) published a shorter version of the same argument with Jackson's authorship and an explicit link to the earlier edition. This public SysCoI post was updated to add that later edition; both belong to one underlying work, not separate new first-live publications.

posts.title: Richard S O’Rourke
posts.description: Richard S O’Rourke sets out a research programme on sustainability that brings energy and material flows into conversation with cybernetic regulation and political economy. His homepage distinguishes thermodynamic entropy from information entropy, and follows a route through Lotka, Ashby, and economic theory. Its research list separates working drafts from published work. This is the same author’s research hub already represented in the atlas; the later SysCoI post also supplies his Substack writing route.

posts.title: Chaos to coordination: vibrating material organises itself into a single rhythm – University of Birmingham (2026)
posts.description: The University of Birmingham reports experiments in which active mechanical units settle into coordinated oscillation through local, non-reciprocal interactions. Initially short waves grow in scale, period, and amplitude until the material moves together. The report describes both a honeycomb assembly and an elastic ring, and calls the process wave coarsening. It provides a concrete physical example of coordination arising from designed interactions. Proposed uses in robotics remain prospective applications of the reported experiments.

posts.title: Up and Down the Ladder of Abstraction: A Systematic Approach to Interactive Visualization – Victor (2011)
posts.description: Bret Victor’s October 2011 interactive essay uses a simple car-control simulation to show how designers can move between a particular run and broader views of possible behaviour. Time and steering parameters can be varied; trajectories expose patterns that are difficult to see during real-time playback. Moving back to a concrete case tests what an abstract picture hides. The essay offers a practical approach to exploring a system when theory is insufficient to predict the consequences of design decisions.

posts.title: The Right to Stop: Epistemic Work-in-Progress and Operational Corrigibility in Lean Systems – Smith
posts.description: Second Law Studio’s first research paper, The Right to Stop, examines Lean practices through the authority to raise evidence and change the operating model. The publisher describes unresolved evidence as epistemic work-in-progress, asking how it is noticed, admitted, assigned, and resolved when correction capacity is overloaded. It proposes operational corrigibility as a capacity for repeated correction. This description is based on the studio’s own public announcement; the paper’s full argument was not independently assessed here.

posts.title: Discovering network resilience formulas with symbolized reinforcement learning – Zheng et al. (2026)
posts.description: Yu Zheng and colleagues report a method that turns learned network-attack strategies into interpretable formulas for assessing resilience. Their account considers both network structure and the dynamical states imposed on it, including the association between node degree and state. The method aims to identify components whose removal can cause a network to fail. The Nature Communications abstract is the basis of this description: the reported performance improvements belong to the authors’ evaluated settings, and do not establish a general measure for every social or organisational use of resilience.

posts.title: Making things change – a free, illustrated, 32-page guide to systems change for young people – Taylor (2026)
posts.description: Benjamin P Taylor's free, illustrated 32-page working draft introduces systems change to younger readers through a fictional student whose unreliable bus leads to an attendance warning. The associated Chosen Path article explains why competing definitions of the problem, institutional rules, authority, power, and different people's experiences matter. Taylor distinguishes the wider systems, cybernetics, and complexity traditions, questions claims that deeper interventions necessarily last longer, and cautions that changing the account of a situation does not itself change timetables, funding, or rules. The guide includes diagrams, a worksheet, references, and a worked example whose results are mixed. Taylor explicitly invites criticism and practical testing.

The paper and course are evolving resources; this entry links the current paper, collection, course, and earlier coverage without treating the author's theoretical claims as established results.

posts.title: Foundations of a postmodern cybernetics based on Kabbalah – Burstein and Negoita (2011)
posts.description: This deliberately grouped SysCoI resource covers two linked works by Gabriel Burstein and Constantin Virgil Negoita. The 2011 Kybernetes paper proposes a Kabbalah Tree of Life-based cybernetic framework for cognition, emotion, and action using feedback, hierarchical control, multi-valued logic, and category theory. Their 2014 chapter develops the proposal for knowledge-based behavioural economics and finance, drawing on system dynamics, emotional intelligence, and tacit knowledge. These are the authors' theoretical propositions, not independent proof that the framework explains or resolves societal problems.

posts.title: VSM simulation ‘Pasta Lasta’ – Lambertz (2026)
posts.description: Mark Lambertz's 'Pasta Lasta' is a facilitated restaurant simulation for exploring Stafford Beer's Viable System Model. Participants organise a fictional hospitality business, respond to an eventful week, and reflect using a VSM laid out on the floor. It foregrounds operational autonomy, coordination, recursion, and decisions under changing conditions. The public guide provides a facilitator handout and alternative session lengths. Lambertz explicitly credits Allenna Leonard for the original storyline.

posts.title: The Third Story of the Universe – Dempsey with Heylighen (2026)
posts.description: Brendan Graham Dempsey talks with cyberneticist Francis Heylighen in a 68-minute Metamodern Meaning episode published on 7 November 2026. These are the speakers' proposed interpretations, not established scientific consensus. The SysCoI post groups the episode with Heylighen's separate Substack as companion reading.

posts.title: Disorder-promoted stability – Montanari et al. (2026)
posts.description: Arthur N. Montanari, Pietro Zanin, and Adilson E. Motter show that heterogeneity among network components or interactions can increase stability in some higher-dimensional dynamical models. The effect depends on the magnitude and location of variation, including non-reciprocal interactions, rather than on disorder being universally helpful. Their theoretical framework discusses neuronal, electrical-grid, material, and ecological networks; it does not establish a general design rule to maximise disorder.

posts.title: Emergence and coexistence of periodic and unstructured motion in future-avoiding random walks – Schmaus et al. (2026)
posts.description: A. Schmaus, K. Stiller, and N. Molkenthin examine mutual future-avoiding random walks, in which stochastic walkers avoid one another's planned future routes instead of their own past movements. Their analysis finds spontaneous periodic behaviour coexisting with unstructured movement and explains the onset through self-amplifying coupling. The paper proposes shared mobility as one possible interpretation, not evidence of an implemented transport service. The public abstract was readable; the complete journal article required subscription access.

posts.title: Pay No Attention to the Model Behind the Curtain – Stark (2022)
posts.description: Philip B. Stark's 2022 paper criticises models used in policy when parameters and assumptions are insufficiently connected to the phenomena they purportedly describe. He challenges placing unlike costs and benefits on a common scale, treating all uncertainties as probabilities and uncritically accepting numerical estimates, using examples from earthquake risk, bird mortality near wind turbines, football penalties, academic gender bias and climate policy. The critique concerns modelling practices, not an argument that all models are invalid.

posts.title: Models and Reality: How Did Models Divorced from Reality Become Epistemologically Acceptable? – Zaman (2020)
posts.description: Asad Zaman (2020) argues that economic models can be judged by formal coherence and conformity to optimisation or equilibrium principles without adequately testing their relationship to the world. He traces this methodological possibility to changes in philosophy of science and the separation of observable phenomena from underlying reality. The paper advances Zaman's contested characterisation of economic modelling; it is not proof that every economic model is divorced from empirical testing.

posts.title: Facing Complexity: Prediction vs. Adaptation – Gershenson (2011)
posts.description: Carlos Gershenson's 2011 paper distinguishes optimising in sufficiently predictable problem spaces from adapting when environments are unpredictable or change rapidly. He argues that interventions can alter the problem they aim to solve, leaving previously optimised responses obsolete. This is his conceptual analysis, not a finding that forecasting or optimisation are always inappropriate.

posts.title: Towards Meta-Renormalisation: The Social Basic – Amonya (2026)
posts.description: FD Amonya's October 2026 nine-page preprint asks when effective descriptions of social processes remain adequate across scales once people adapt within, and alter, the conditions of future adaptation. It proposes the relationally constituted 'Social Basic' and a formal exact/approximate coarse-grained closure criterion, while distinguishing participants' operative representations from analysts' models. The public SysCoI commentary explains the mathematical test and its possible second-order cybernetic relevance, but notes that empirical scale transformations, measures, tolerances and universality results have not yet been demonstrated. The original paper's ResearchGate and SSRN reading routes were not independently accessible during this intake.

posts.title: A ‘Good Regulator Theorem’ for Embodied Agents – Virgo et al. (2025)
posts.description: Nathaniel Virgo, Martin Biehl, Manuel Baltieri and Matteo Capucci revisit the Conant–Ashby good regulator theorem for embodied agents. Their formulation allows an observer to interpret successful regulation as belief updating about the environment: a model is attributed through an interpretation map rather than necessarily present as a literal internal representation. The model may be trivial, accommodating apparently model-free regulators. The formal treatment uses deterministic discrete-time systems, and does not establish that each effective regulator has a rich internal model.

She presents the approaches as promising tools for research and more inclusive deliberation, rather than reporting a completed evaluation.

posts.title: The Equilibrium of Delay – 42 The Systemic Review (2026)
posts.description: 42 The Systemic Review analyses the recurring City of Playford capital-works backlog in Australia as a stock-and-flow problem involving accumulating commitments, planning-and-design capacity, and feedback from delayed work. The paper argues that finance-based prioritisation lacks the response variety needed for different kinds of infrastructure demand, and proposes matching commitments to real delivery capacity while addressing unmet infrastructure needs. These are the publisher's systemic interpretation and proposed interventions, not findings independently validated against all underlying council evidence.

posts.title: Survey of Riffs and Rotes • 1
posts.description: Jon Awbrey's 'Survey of Riffs and Rotes • 1' brings together the OEIS wiki hub, five linked blog dialogues from 2013 to 2020, annual series posts, and other explorations of his Riff and Rote method. His introduction places that method in the context of generalized primes and combinatorial constructions, referring to it as an instance of his 'Make A Picture' approach. The linked OEIS wiki defines doubly recursive prime factorisation and its graph representations. This post is a reading guide to the existing material, not a new independently validated mathematical result.
